item.research_question: How can strong local compositional disorder in high entropy oxides be exploited to generate tunable magnetic behaviors, ranging from macroscopically ordered states to frustration-driven dynamic spin interactions, and can a simplified model predict the emergence of these states?
item.material_system: La(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2)O3 (L5BO) and Mn-varied variants La(Cr0.15Mn0.4Fe0.15Co0.15Ni0.15)O3 (40% Mn) and La(Cr0.1Mn0.6Fe0.1Co0.1Ni0.1)O3 (60% Mn)
item.processing_route: Pulsed laser epitaxy (PLD) on SrTiO3 (STO) and (La0.3Sr0.7)(Al0.65Ta0.35)O3 (LSAT) substrates; films were single-phase, epitaxial, with thicknesses of 56 nm (40% Mn), 58 nm (60% Mn), 62 nm (20% Mn), and ~90 nm for neutron diffraction.
item.test_conditions: Neutron diffraction on single-crystal films and bulk powder; SQUID magnetometry (field-cooled vs. zero-field-cooled) from low temperatures up to 300 K; Monte Carlo simulations using a classical Heisenberg model.
key_findings: L5BO (20% Mn) exhibits robust long-range G-type antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering with a Néel temperature (T_N) near 180 K in single-crystal films.
Increasing Mn concentration to 40% creates a degenerate tipping point where both AFM and ferromagnetic (FM) phases are percolated, resulting in a horizontal exchange bias shift.
Increasing Mn concentration to 60% shifts the dominant phase to ferromagnetism with a Curie temperature (T_C) of approximately 160 K and no observable exchange bias.
The 20% Mn system shows a vertical loop shift due to uncompensated FM moments within a percolated AFM matrix.
The 40% Mn composition displays an incipient quantum critical point where AFM and FM signals grow simultaneously upon cooling.
A classical Heisenberg model populated with composite parameter states accurately predicted the magnetic phase diagram and critical temperatures.
Exchange bias behaviors, traditionally found in bilayer heterojunctions, were generated in monolithic single-crystal films by manipulating local spin disorder.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the high entropy oxide hosts a random distribution of spin (S) and exchange (J) interactions where the dominant magnetic phase is determined by the percolation of specific microstates. Increasing Mn concentration shifts the balance from AFM-dominant (Fe-O-Fe bonds) to FM-dominant (Mn-O-X bonds). At 40% Mn, the system reaches a state where both AFM and FM clusters percolate coherently, creating intrinsic frustration and uncompensated spins at the interface of these coexisting phases, which drives the exchange bias effect without the need for physical heterostructuring.
item.limitations: The text notes that computationally intensive first-principles approaches are impractical for high entropy oxides due to the vast number of possible microstates (over 200 nearest neighbor combinations), necessitating the use of a simplified classical Heisenberg model rather than precise quantitative calculations.
item.future_work: The authors propose that manipulating local spin disorder can be used to design novel Griffiths phases or quantum many-body systems with tunable critical behaviors, and that replacing geometric frustration with exchange frustration on a square lattice may lead to unexpected phase spaces.
quotes: Single‐crystal La(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2)O3 films are used as a model system hosting a magnetic sublattice with a high degree of microstate disorder in the form of site‐to‐site spin and exchange type inhomogeneity.

Model‐predicted materials are synthesized and found to possess an incipient quantum critical point when magnetic ordering types are designed to be in direct competition, this leads to highly controllable exchange bias behaviors previously accessible only in intentionally designed bilayer heterojunctions.
The horizontal shift in magnetization is clear evidence of the traditional exchange biasing behavior associated with coexisting and coupled FM and AFM phases of similar energy scale.
